title: Comparative evaluation of handheld vs. high-end ultrasound systems for TIPSS hemodynamic assessment: first impressions.
abstract: Background Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPSS) procedures require reliable post-interventional hemodynamic monitoring to detect shunt dysfunction, for which Doppler ultrasonography is the preferred modality. Owing to the rapid development of handheld ultrasound devices, their diagnostic equivalence to high-end systems warrants investigation. Materials and methods A pilot group of 23 patients (n = 13 males, 65%; n = 7 females; 35%; n = 3 unknown) with intrahepatic TIPSS were retrospectively analyzed. Blood flow measurements were obtained and compared using a high-end ultrasound system (Resona R9, Mindray) and modern handheld ultrasound device (Vscan Air™ CL, GE). The TIPSS was evaluated using B-mode and color Doppler sonography. Image quality was assessed using a 5-point scale and flow parameters using statistical analysis. The image quality and the difference between the two devices were analyzed using correlation coefficients and multivariable linear regression models including TIPSS flow values, skin-to-TIPSS distance, and TIPSS dwell time. Results Both devices produced clinically interpretable images. However, the high-end device yielded superior image quality in 16 of 23 cases (p < 0.001). Significant correlations were observed between the difference in mean TIPSS flow measurements obtained by the two devices (Δ mean TIPSS flow) and corresponding average flow values measured by the two devices (Kendall's τ = 0.656; p < 0.001). Significant associations with Δ TIPSS mean flow were identified for skin-to-TIPSS distance (τ = 0.39; p = 0.014) and TIPSS dwell time (τ = -0.39; p = 0.017). In multivariable analysis, both mean TIPSS flow measured by the high-end system and skin-to-TIPSS distance remained significantly associated with Δ TIPSS mean flow. The TIPSS mean flow measured by the high-end system correlated with TIPSS dwell time (τ = 0.38; p = 0.021). Bland-Altman analysis revealed that handheld measurements tended to overestimate low flows and underestimate high flows. Conclusion Handheld ultrasound devices show promising potential for TIPSS surveillance; however, they could lead to distorted flow deviations. Contemporary handheld devices may nevertheless be useful in selected point-of-care settings but cannot yet replace high-end systems for precise hemodynamic monitoring. Larger prospective studies are required. Trial registration No clinical trial registration was performed, as this study is a single-center retrospective observational analysis based on existing clinical data. The study did not involve prospective patient enrollment, international procedures, or assignment to treatment groups. Therefore, registration in a clinical trial registry was not applicable.

title: Preoperative prediction of lymphovascular space invasion in early-stage cervical cancer using a deep learning-based 3D super-resolution MRI radiomics model.
abstract: Background Lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI) is a critical prognostic factor guiding adjuvant therapy in early-stage cervical cancer, yet its preoperative assessment is often limited by the spatial resolution of standard MRI. This study aimed to investigate the value of a deep learning-based 3D super-resolution (SR) MRI radiomics model in predicting LVSI and to evaluate how SR reconstruction impacts image quality and radiomic feature robustness. Methods This retrospective study included 117 patients with early-stage cervical cancer (training cohort: n = 81; validation cohort: n = 36). A 3D Super-Resolution Generative Adversarial Network (SRGAN) reconstructed T2-SPAIR and DWI sequences into super-resolution images (SRI) with a 4× upsampling factor. Radiomic features were extracted, and an SRI-based multimodal fusion model was developed and systematically compared with original image (OI)-based and clinical models using the Area Under the Curve (AUC) and Decision Curve Analysis (DCA). Results SR reconstruction significantly improved the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for both DWI (P = 0.012) and T2-SPAIR (P = 0.030). For DWI, SRI preserved intratumoral texture heterogeneity, leading to improved diagnostic performance (Validation AUC: SRI-DWI 0.864 vs. OI-DWI 0.727, P = 0.041). The final SRI-Fusion model achieved the highest diagnostic accuracy (Validation AUC: 0.934), significantly outperforming the OI-Fusion model (AUC: 0.828, P = 0.044) and the clinical model (AUC: 0.626, P = 0.012). Conclusions SRGAN-based reconstruction effectively improves MRI quality and feature robustness, particularly in DWI. The SRI-based multimodal radiomics model demonstrates superior predictive performance for LVSI in early-stage cervical cancer compared to conventional imaging and clinical models.

title: Can radiomics outperform radiologists in predicting Ewing sarcoma response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy from longitudinal MRI?
abstract: Objective This retrospective, multicenter study evaluated whether MRI-based radiomics can predict the histological response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in Ewing sarcoma patients and compared their performance to that of radiological findings. Definitive histological assessment is only possible during surgery, potentially delaying therapy changes and increasing metastatic risk; therefore, a positive outcome would enable early adaptations. Methods Radiomics features were extracted from pre- and post-neoadjuvant (after first chemotherapy cycle) chemotherapy scans of patients treated from 2004 to 2020. Four machine learning models were trained using nested cross-validation to predict histological response, and their performance was compared to models trained on semantic features derived from expert radiological readings. Diagnostic performance was measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Results 96 patients (mean age, 19.9 ± 11.7 years; 41 women) with Ewing sarcoma were evaluated. Radiomics features related to low gray level intensity changes in T1 fat-saturated contrast-enhanced sequences showed the highest responder identification performance (AUROC, 0.62; 95% CI: 0.59, 0.65), surpassing the best radiological model, which relied on the relative change in maximum diameter of extratumoral soft tissue components (AUROC, 0.58; 95% CI: 0.56, 0.60). Radiomics models relying on pre-treatment T2-weighted data performed similarly (AUROC, 0.61; 95% CI: 0.58, 0.64), outperforming the clinical baseline (AUROC, 0.53; 95% CI: 0.51, 0.55). Conclusion MRI-based radiomics moderately identified responders to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, suggesting a role for earlier, tailored therapeutic strategies in Ewing sarcoma. Larger studies to validate these findings within a multimodal framework are warranted. Clinical relevance statement Radiomics extracted from MRI scans may aid with non-size tissue signals in early prediction of neoadjuvant chemotherapy response in Ewing sarcoma patients, potentially guiding personalized treatment adaptations, reducing delays for non-responders, and improving patient outcomes. These exploratory findings are complementary to standard size-based assessment from clinical routine, and warrant larger, prospective trials to be established.

title: Multimodal imaging features of atypical multifocal torpedo maculopathy: a case report.
abstract: Background Torpedo maculopathy (TM) is a rare congenital retinal abnormality, typically presenting as a solitary, torpedo-shaped hypopigmented lesion located temporal to the fovea with its apex pointing toward the fovea. Multifocal TM is exceedingly uncommon, and its multimodal imaging characteristics and lesion distribution remain incompletely understood. Case presentation A 32-year-old man was referred after an incidental abnormality was detected in the fundus of his right eye. He was asymptomatic, with uncorrected visual acuity of 20/20 in both eyes. Color fundus photography revealed a typical torpedo-shaped lesion temporal to the macula and additional elongated temporal lesions with indistinct borders. OCT demonstrated focal RPE attenuation or loss, increased choroidal hypertransmission, and outer retinal involvement, with a slit-like subretinal cleft in one lesion. FFA showed multiple well-demarcated hyperfluorescent lesions without leakage, whereas ICGA revealed corresponding hypofluorescent areas and provided clearer delineation of lesion margins and extent. These findings supported the diagnosis of atypical multifocal torpedo maculopathy. Given the absence of symptoms and preserved visual function, no treatment was required and periodic follow-up was recommended. Conclusions Multifocal TM may show atypical morphology on color fundus photography, with some lesions appearing poorly demarcated and their extent potentially underestimated. Integrated multimodal imaging, particularly OCT, FFA, and ICGA, enables a more comprehensive assessment of lesion morphology, distribution, and structural heterogeneity. Among these modalities, ICGA may provide additional value in delineating lesion boundaries and extent. This case further expands the imaging spectrum of multifocal TM and highlights the importance of integrated multimodal imaging in atypical presentations.

title: When a glabellar dermoid cyst is not the whole story: the significance of MRI in excluding intracranial segments.
abstract: Background Epidermoid and dermoid cysts are one of the most common benign pediatric tumors of the skull. Ultrasonography is usually the diagnostic tool of choice for their evaluation and diagnosis. Although benign, local growth with cosmetic issues, bone erosion, and occasional intracranial involvement generally warrant surgical resection. Since epidermoid and dermoid cysts may be seen by a wide range of medical disciplines, standardized recommendations for optimal diagnosis and treatment are necessary. Case presentation We report the case of a 14-month-old boy, who underwent neurosurgical removal of a glabellar dermoid cyst classified as an extracranial lesion, and in whom an intracranial lesion was identified on follow-up MRI, represents a rare and unusual clinical course. Ten months after surgery, a surveillance MRI revealed an intracranial lesion in the right frontal parasagittal region, while the child had developed no symptoms. Very careful retrospective review of the initial MRI suggested that an extremely small intracranial part of the lesion might have been faintly visible upon knowledge of the further clinical course. The intracranial lesion was subsequently resected and diagnosed as an epidermoid cyst. In our mini-review, we have compiled evidence that intracranial extension is more common than expected and particularly occurs in craniofacial midline lesions but is definitely not restricted to them. Conclusion Together, this case and literature review highlight the importance of careful preoperative assessment and interdisciplinary discussion to adequately determine the extent of craniofacial dermoid and epidermoid cysts before surgery. This case illustrates that a subtle intracranial lesion may not be recognizable on initial image interpretation despite MRI having been performed. Imaging follow-up is definitely recommended when intraoperative findings raise concern about deeper extension.

title: MRI-based assessment of greater tuberosity exposure in massive rotator cuff tears: a systematic review of current evidence and methodological gaps.
abstract: Background Massive rotator cuff tears (MRCTs) lack a standardized and reproducible imaging-based definition. A recent Delphi consensus introduced greater tuberosity exposure (GTE) as a defining criterion for MRCTs, proposing that MRCTs be classified by either involvement of at least two rotator cuff tendons or ≥ 67% GTE on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Purpose To evaluate the role of GTE in the MRI-based definition and structural characterization of MRCTs and to describe the extent and methodological maturity of the evidence available for GTE and established MRI-derived parameters. Methods A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from database inception to February 17, 2026, and updated on October 9 and 11, 2026 with supplementary citation searching, in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies were included if they investigated MRCTs using MRI-based or MRI-transferable imaging and reported structural definitions, measurement methods, or associations with irreparability, structural healing, or clinical outcomes. Prognostic studies were assessed using the Quality In Prognosis Studies (QUIPS) tool. Findings were synthesized narratively; no meta-analysis was performed due to substantial heterogeneity in study designs, imaging protocols, and outcome definitions. The synthesis described the extent and methodological maturity of the available evidence and did not compare diagnostic or prognostic performance between parameters. Results A total of 34 studies were included. No study evaluated GTE as a quantitative MRI-derived parameter. Only two studies addressed footprint coverage on imaging, one qualitatively and one by a semi-quantitative five-zone score of residual tendon attachment; neither measured GTE as a defined exposure parameter or applied predefined thresholds. In contrast, MRCTs were consistently characterized using indirect structural parameters, primarily tendon involvement and tear size. Established MRI-derived variables-including tear size, tendon retraction, fatty infiltration, muscle atrophy, and superior humeral migration-were assessed using established measurement frameworks based on defined anatomical landmarks, notwithstanding methodological heterogeneity in imaging protocols and thresholds across studies. These parameters were frequently evaluated in relation to irreparability, structural healing, and functional outcomes, whereas no study evaluated a direct quantitative MRI-based measure of GTE in relation to a clinical or structural endpoint. Conclusion No standardized and outcome-validated MRI-based method for quantifying GTE was identified within the scope of this review. Despite its conceptual appeal as a direct representation of footprint deficiency, GTE has not yet undergone standardized measurement development or outcome-based validation. The evidence base for established MRI-derived parameters is more extensive and methodologically mature, with operationalized measurement methods and reported outcome associations; this does not imply clinical inferiority of GTE. Future research should focus on developing reproducible MRI-based measurement techniques for GTE and evaluating its diagnostic and prognostic relevance in dedicated validation studies. Study design Systematic review; Level of evidence, 3. Individual included studies ranged from Level II to Level V.

title: Clinical accuracy of transferring virtually planned zygomatic implant positions in severely atrophic maxilla: a single-arm study.
abstract: Objectives This study aimed to evaluate the clinical accuracy of transferring virtually planned zygomatic implant positions in severely atrophic maxilla. Materials and methods This clinical accuracy study included 24 participants with severely atrophic edentulous maxilla. All cases were digitally planned using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) and treated with bilateral zygomatic implants under general anesthesia, with additional anterior conventional implants. Postoperative CBCT was used to superimpose the actual implant positions onto the virtual plan and assess coronal and apical deviations. Results A total of 48 zygomatic implants were placed in 24 participants. Three-dimensional superimposition of the preoperative virtual plans and postoperative CBCT scans demonstrated a mean coronal deviation of 1.917 ± 0.401 mm overall, with values of 1.989 ± 0.540 mm on the right side and 1.846 ± 0.160 mm on the left side. The overall mean apical deviation was 1.733 ± 0.429 mm, with values of 1.757 ± 0.172 mm on the right side and 1.709 ± 0.588 mm on the left side. Conclusions Virtual surgical planning enabled the transfer of planned zygomatic implant positions with measurable coronal and apical deviations. These findings describe short-term positional accuracy and should not be interpreted as evidence of long-term implant stability, treatment efficacy, or overall safety. Trial registration Trial was retrospectively registered on 31/03/2023 at Pan African Clinical Trials Registry ( https://pactr.samrc.ac.za ) (ID: PACTR202603707948061) under the following link: https://pactr.samrc.ac.za/TrialDisplay.aspx?TrialID=40945 .

title: Assessment of an artificial intelligence model designed for prediction of lateral cephalometric measurements from lateral photographs.
abstract: Background Lateral cephalometric analysis is necessary for proper orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning. Classically it depends upon manual landmark identification on radiographs, which is time consuming, relies on expert skills. Accordingly, this study aimed to create and evaluate a deep learning model for automated cephalometric assessment using lateral profile photographs as a radiation free alternative. Materials & methods A total of 1,350 dataset was used to train a dual task model using HRNetV2 combined with an Adaptive Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) to predict 19 landmark coordinates. The model was tested using 150 unseen photographs to evaluate the Mean Radial Error (MRE), Successful Detection Rate (SDR), Mean Absolute Error of the angular and linear measurements and classification accuracy. Results The HRNetV2 + MLP model combination achieved a mean radial error of 2.317 ± 1.80 mm, with SDRs at the 2 mm and 4 mm thresholds were 53.8% and 84.5%, respectively. The ANB angle demonstrated Mean absolute error of 1.46º. Bland-Altman analysis revealed minimal systematic bias between AI and Dolphin measurements across most cephalometric variables. Conclusion These findings demonstrate the feasibility of automated landmark detection and analysis from lateral facial photographs and support further investigation of the photographic-based approaches thus eliminating radiographic exposures.

title: Patient-specific three-dimensional titanium plate versus conventional two-miniplate fixation for mandibular angle fractures: a randomized clinical trial.
abstract: Background Mandibular angle fractures are clinically challenging because of their anatomical complexity and biomechanical loading. Conventional two-miniplate fixation requires intraoperative plate adaptation and transbuccal instrumentation. Patient-specific three-dimensional titanium plates are designed to conform to individual mandibular anatomy and may facilitate intraoperative fixation. This study aimed to clinically and radiographically evaluate patient-specific three-dimensional titanium plate versus conventional two mini-plate fixation in the management of mandibular angle fractures. Methods Sixteen patients with recent mandibular angle fractures were randomly allocated into two equal groups (n = 8). Group I underwent fixation using a patient-specific three-dimensional titanium plate positioned according to the preoperative virtual plan, whereas Group II received conventional two-miniplate fixation. The primary outcome was functional recovery assessed by maximal mouth opening (MMO). Secondary outcomes included intraoperative time, postoperative pain, facial edema, postoperative occlusion, wound healing, and CT bone density measurements in Hounsfield units (HU). Clinical outcomes were evaluated on postoperative days 1, 7, 14, and 30, whereas bone density was assessed immediately postoperatively and after 4 months. Results Intraoperative time was shorter in the patient-specific plate group than in the conventional two-miniplate group (40.00 ± 9.35 vs. 73.25 ± 11.22 min; P < 0.001). Postoperative pain was lower in the patient-specific plate group on postoperative day 1 (P = 0.015), while facial edema was lower on postoperative days 1 (P = 0.012) and 7 (P = 0.031). No statistically significant between-group differences were detected in maximal mouth opening, postoperative occlusion, Landry wound healing index scores, or CT bone density at the four-month follow-up. One patient in each group developed wound dehiscence, with complete healing after conservative management. Conclusions Patient-specific three-dimensional titanium plate fixation was associated with shorter intraoperative time and lower early postoperative pain and edema. No statistically significant between-group differences were detected in the other assessed clinical and radiographic outcomes during the four-month follow-up. Trial registration The study was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07390734) on 29 January 2026.

title: Association between periodontitis and coronary plaque composition: can early periodontal treatment influence coronary artery disease progression? A study protocol for a prospective, randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Objective The (PERIOdontitis and Coronary Artery Disease) PERIOCAD study aims to investigate the association between periodontitis and coronary artery disease (CAD) in patients undergoing cardiac computed tomography angiography (CCTA) and the effectiveness of early versus late periodontitis (PD) treatment on systemic inflammation and CAD progression. Background PD and CAD are common diseases, sharing underlying molecular mechanisms, like systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction. Epidemiological and genetic studies suggest a strong link between PD and CAD. Yet, it remains unclear whether treatment of periodontitis may attenuate progression of arteriosclerosis. CCTA enables reproducible quantitative assessment of coronary plaque volumes and composition, providing metrics for both cross-sectional associations and longitudinal changes of plaque burden. Methods PERIOCAD is a prospective, randomized, controlled trial (RCT) aiming to enroll 200 patients who undergo clinically indicated CCTA. All participants will undergo comprehensive periodontal status assessment and patients diagnosed with PD (estimated n = 100) will be randomized 1:1 to either early, systematic PD therapy (intervention arm) or delayed care after 2 years (control arm). CCTA analysis will include quantitative plaque volumes and composition, assessment of high-risk plaque features and evaluation of pericoronary adipose tissue attenuation (PCAT). Cardiac and inflammatory biomarkers will be assessed at baseline and after 24 months. Follow-up evaluations are scheduled at 12 and 24 months to reassess periodontal status. In addition, changes in plaque burden will be longitudinally assessed in case of clinically indicated repeat CCTA scans. The primary endpoint is the influence of periodontal treatment on cardiac and inflammatory biomarkers at 24 months. Secondary endpoints include major adverse cardiovascular events during follow-up, changes in plaque parameters and PCAT on serial CCTA, and associations between CCTA metrics and PD at baseline. Discussion PERIOCAD is expected to provide unique insights regarding the relationship between PD and CAD, being to our knowledge the first RCT to investigate the impact of PD therapy on systemic inflammation and CAD progression in symptomatic patients. Our findings could have significant implications for interdisciplinary cardiovascular disease prevention strategies and public health policies. Trial registration German Clinical Trials Register DRKS00038470 (Date of registration:2025-11-24).

title: The law of surprise: temporal variation and seasonality of acute aortic syndromes: a single-centre epidemiologic cohort analysis spanning 20 years.
abstract: Background and aims Acute aortic syndromes (AAS) represent life-threatening cardiovascular emergencies characterized by high mortality rates despite rapid intervention. Global epidemiological data indicate substantial variance in incidence. Longitudinal single-centre data over extended periods are limited but crucial for understanding diagnostic, demographic, and systemic factors influencing admission trends.(1). This study aimed to analyze annual and seasonal variation trends of AAS over a 20-year period in a single maximal care centre and explore potential chronological and environmental contributors to this variation. Methods This retrospective cohort study evaluated 403 patients admitted with a confirmed diagnosis of AAS between 2005 and 2025 at the University Hospital Erlangen, Germany. All diagnoses were established via computed tomography angiography (CTA) and confirmed intraoperatively. Annual, quarterly, and monthly surgical volumes were calculated, and temporal trends were analyzed using Poisson and negative binomial regression models. Admission rates during public holidays and school vacations were also evaluated. Results Over the 20-year observation period, a steady increasing trend in the annual number of AAS cases was observed, peaking in 2017. Analysis of quarterly distributions revealed a statistically significant dominance of cases in the fourth quarter (Q4: October-December; p < 0.05) compared to the second (Q2) and third (Q3) quarters. Monthly analysis demonstrated a prominent peak in October (incidence rate ratio [IRR] = 1.85 vs. June, p < 0.05). Conversely, fixed public holidays and school vacations were associated with statistically significant reductions in daily admission counts (p < 0.05), with the lowest relative case counts observed during the Christmas vacation period (IRR: 0.40-0.50). Conclusion The case counts of acute aortic syndromes exhibits significant temporal and seasonal variation, characterized by a distinct late-autumn and early-winter peak, alongside significant declines during institutional vacation periods. These findings suggest that acute cardiovascular events are heavily modulated by cyclical environmental and socio-systemic factors.

title: Computed tomography anatomy of the pony thorax and abdomen and an example of a clinical application.
abstract: Background In veterinary medicine, computed tomography (CT) is a valuable diagnostic tool that provides detailed cross-sectional images with higher contrast resolution than conventional radiography. However, owing to the large body-size of horses, CT has been primarily limited in equine veterinary practice to imaging of the head, neck, and extremities, as imaging studies of the thoracic and abdominal cavities are not possible with standard gantry size in medium-to-large horses. In this study, we aimed to characterise the normal thoracic and abdominal anatomy of ponies using CT and to describe an example of the potential clinical applications of abdominal CT. CT examination of two ponies was performed in dorsal recumbency using a helical 16-slice multidetector scanner with a 90 cm-diameter gantry. The normal anatomy of these cavities was described and compared with anatomical cross-sections, and a clinical case involving colic surgery was analysed. Results Most of the thoracic and abdominal organs in the anatomical section were identifiable, and the use of these images as a reference assisted well in the interpretation of the clinical case scans. The advanced imaging technique aided in surgical planning. In the case involving colic surgery, no evidence of thick-walled intestinal segments was found on CT, but contents including gas, fluid, different types of ingests, and sand were identified preoperatively. Nerves or serous membranes (except for the spinal cord) could not be clearly identified on native CT images. Conclusions CT was useful for clinical diagnosis, but the small number of cases included in the study is a limitation that should be acknowledged.

title: Considerations on external validation, potential data leakage, and model selection in a PET/CT-based radiomics model predicting residual disease in ovarian cancer.
abstract: Ye et al. recently reported that a PET/CT-based radiomics model incorporating clinical variables and using a support vector machine classifier outperformed conventional scoring systems in predicting complete cytoreduction in ovarian cancer (J Ovarian Res 2026). We appreciate this valuable contribution and wish to raise three points for consideration. First, although the validation cohort was held out from model development, it shares institution and scanner platform with part of the training set. The Siemens platform, which contributed 103 of 153 training patients, was not represented in the validation cohort. The results may therefore primarily reflect reproducibility on the GE platform, and broader cross-center or cross-scanner generalizability may warrant further evaluation. Second, SMOTE oversampling and mRMR feature selection are described as applied to the entire training cohort before nested cross-validation; if this reflects the actual workflow, fold-level data leakage could be a consideration. Third, selecting the SVM from seven models using identical cross-validation estimates and reporting the maximum could, in principle, introduce some optimistic selection bias. These points are offered in the hope of further strengthening the evidence base for broader multicenter use.

title: CT-based radiomics for interpretable outcome prediction after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: a multicenter cohort study.
abstract: Background Prognostic assessment after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) mainly relies on clinical variables and computed tomography (CT) findings, but current models often lack biological interpretability. We developed and validated a clinical-radiomics prognostic model and subsequently performed exploratory cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) proteomic characterization of model-defined risk phenotypes. Methods This multicenter cohort from the PROSAH-MPC registry included 879 patients across four hospitals. Patients from the primary center were split into training (n = 637) and internal validation (n = 160) cohorts, while patients from three other centers formed an external validation cohort (n = 82). Admission CT hemorrhagic lesions were automatically segmented using the validated BrainHemoAI platform, and radiomic features were extracted with PyRadiomics. Clinical, radiomics, and combined clinical-radiomics XGBoost models were developed and interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Risk scores from the clinical-radiomics model were applied to an independent prospective enrichment, gene setCSF​ proteomic cohort to define combined model-based high- and low-risk groups. Gene Ontology (GO)/ Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), and protein-protein interaction (PPI) analyses were performed. Results The combined model yielded AUCs of 0.892 and 0.820 in the internal test and external validation cohorts, respectively. Risk reclassification analyses suggested that radiomic features may provide complementary prognostic information. SHAP identified radiomic heterogeneity and key clinical variables as major predictors. Meanwhile, exploratory CSF proteomic analysis identified candidate differentially expressed proteins and associated pathway signals that differed between groups defined by high and low combined clinical-radiomics risk scores. Conclusions This clinical-radiomics prognostic model enables accurate outcome prediction and provides exploratory biological insight into unfavorable recovery after aSAH, supporting refined risk stratification and potential targeted therapeutic development. Trial registration PROSAH-MPC. NCT05738083. Registered 16 November 2022 - Retrospectively registered, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05738083 .

title: Depth-specific characterization of bone microarchitecture in the femoral head: implications for osteoarthritis and osteoporosis research.
abstract: Background Osteoarthritis (OA) and osteoporosis (OP) are highly prevalent musculoskeletal diseases characterized by cartilage loss and increased subchondral bone formation and by systemic bone mass reduction, respectively. The femoral head is commonly examined in both OA and OP research, yet both conditions may coexist in the same patient, making it unclear how local cartilage degeneration and systemic bone mineral density (BMD), as a marker of OP-related skeletal status, contribute to bone microarchitectural changes at different depths. Methods Femoral heads were obtained from 30 patients undergoing primary total hip arthroplasty for hip OA. Ex vivo high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HR-pQCT) was performed on the entire femoral head, followed by computational segmentation of the subchondral mineralized plate (SMP) and five concentric trabecular regions. Depth-specific bone microarchitectural parameters were analyzed in relation to histologically assessed cartilage degeneration and systemic BMD measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Results The cohort had a mean age of 75.4 ± 9.5 years, 53.3% were female, and patients spanned the spectrum of normal BMD (36.7%), osteopenia (46.7%), and osteoporosis (16.7%). Trabecular volumetric tissue mineral density (Tb.vTMD), bone volume to tissue volume (BV/TV), and trabecular thickness (Tb.Th) showed an initial decrease in the superficial trabecular regions, followed by a progressive increase toward deeper regions, whereas cyst-like void volume continuously decreased with depth and almost completely disappeared beyond 9.84 mm in depth. Cartilage degeneration independently predicted subchondral bone microstructure within the SMP and in superficial to intermediate trabecular regions (up to 13.12 mm in depth). Specifically, higher OARSI grades were associated with higher SMP.Th, Tb.vTMD, BV/TV, and Tb.Th. Systemic BMD T-score emerged as an independent predictor of trabecular bone parameters across all depths and represented the sole determinant of BV/TV and Tb.Th in the deepest trabecular region (beyond 13.12 mm depth), while cartilage degeneration was not associated with trabecular bone parameters in the deepest trabecular region. Conclusions Our findings showcase spatially distinct contributions of cartilage degeneration and systemic skeletal status to subchondral bone remodeling, identifying depth as a critical determinant in the analysis of osteochondral alterations in hip OA. Specifically, our findings emphasize that systemic BMD should be considered a covariate in OA research and that deep regions of the femoral head should be used for OP research to minimize potential confounding by local OA-related effects.

title: Quantitative imaging-pathology correlation in nodular fasciitis and diagnostic discrimination from sarcoma.
abstract: Objectives To investigate associations between key magnetic resonance imaging features of nodular fasciitis (NF) and quantitative histopathologic biomarkers, and to evaluate whether their integration provides complementary information for differentiating NF from soft tissue sarcoma (STS) in diagnostically equivocal settings. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 128 patients with NF and 133 with STS who underwent preoperative 3-T MRI between May 2023 and June 2025. Two blinded musculoskeletal radiologists independently evaluated predefined imaging features, including fascial tail sign, T2 heterogeneity score, enhancement pattern, perilesional edema, and mean/minimum apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC). Histopathology quantified cellular density, collagen content, and myxoid degeneration. Imaging-pathology correlations were assessed using Spearman analysis and multivariable regression. Diagnostic performance of MRI-only, pathology-only, and combined models was evaluated using logistic regression, receiver operating characteristic (ROC), area under the curve (AUC) analysis, calibration, decision curve analysis, and bootstrap validation. Results T2 heterogeneity correlated positively with myxoid degeneration (ρ = 0.52) and negatively with collagen content (ρ = -0.28) (p < 0.001). Mean ADC correlated inversely with cellular density (ρ = -0.63, p < 0.001). Mean ADC was significantly higher in NF than STS (p < 0.001). The combined model outperformed MRI alone (AUC, 0.96 vs 0.89) and demonstrated greater net clinical benefit. Bootstrap validation confirmed stable performance (mean AUC, 0.960; 95% confidence interval, 0.938-0.978). Conclusion Imaging features of NF were associated with underlying stromal and cellular substrates. Integrating imaging features with quantitative pathology biomarkers may support radiology-pathology concordance assessment in selected diagnostically equivocal cases. Key points Question How can we improve radiology-pathology concordance and reduce interpretative variability for NF cases presenting with suspicious, diagnostically equivocal magnetic resonance imaging findings? Findings T2 heterogeneity and diffusion measurements are associated with stromal composition and cellularity, while predefined MRI features demonstrated substantial-to-excellent inter-reader agreement. Critical relevance statement Embedding explicit AHA criteria in the prompt let an 8B model approach 671B-model agreement (38.91-81.52%), supporting standardized text-based workflows without fine-tuning.

title: MRI-based deep-learning radiomics nomogram for differentiating FIGO 2023 stage I from stage II-IV endometrial cancer: a multicenter study.
abstract: Objectives Preoperative identification of FIGO 2023 stage I endometrial cancer (EC) is important for treatment planning. We aimed to develop and validate a deep-learning radiomics nomogram (DLRN) based on multiparametric MRI to distinguish stage I EC from stage II-IV disease. Materials and methods This study retrospectively enrolled patients from three centers. Patients from Centers 1 and 2 were randomly split into a training set (n = 616), and an internal test set (n = 158), and Center 3 served as an external test set (n = 232). The DLRN integrated deep-learning features, intratumoral and peritumoral radiomics features, and clinical characteristics. The DLRN was compared with clinical, radiomics, and deep-learning models. Discrimination was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with AUCs compared using DeLong's test. Results A total of 1006 patients (mean age, 56.5 ± 9.7 years) were analyzed. In the internal test set, the DLRN achieved an AUC of 0.852, higher than the clinical (0.673; p = 0.001), original radiomics (0.765; p = 0.030), and combined radiomics (0.793; p = 0.050) models. In the external test set, the DLRN remained robust (AUC = 0.829) and outperformed the clinical, original radiomics, and combined radiomics models (AUC = 0.680, 0.681, and 0.743; all p < 0.005). With DLRN assistance, radiologists showed improved diagnostic performance. Conclusion The MRI-based DLRN showed robust discrimination between FIGO 2023 stage I and stage II-IV EC across test sets, supporting its potential for preoperative risk stratification and decision support. Key points Question The introduction of the FIGO 2023 staging system has made the differentiation between stages more challenging, highlighting the need for better tools. Findings A new MRI-based deep-learning radiomics nomogram (DLRN) accurately identifies high-risk patients, significantly outperforming traditional and individual clinical prediction methods. Critical relevance statement This tool helps doctors make better preoperative treatment plans, potentially improving patient outcomes in endometrial cancer.

title: Predatory publishing in radiology: advice for early-career researchers.
abstract: Predatory journals typically use practices based on deceit, misleading information, lack of transparency, and the absence of rigorous peer review. Within radiology, such journals frequently publish articles with minimal editorial oversight and limited scientific credibility. The relevance of this issue in radiology has grown as imaging research has expanded rapidly, particularly in artificial intelligence (AI), quantitative imaging, and subspecialty-driven innovation. Given the academic pressure created by the "publish or perish" culture, this environment makes early-career radiologists especially vulnerable to predatory journals that promise rapid publication and high acceptance rates. Predatory journals exploit this environment by sending unsolicited invitations to publish or join editorial boards, frequently using flattering language and promising unrealistic publication timelines. These journals generally lack robust peer review, methodological scrutiny, and transparency and are typically not indexed in established databases such as PubMed, Scopus, or Web of Science. Consequently, articles published in these outlets have reduced visibility, limited citation potential, and minimal impact on radiological science or clinical practice. Furthermore, publication in predatory journals may adversely affect academic reputation and career advancement, as hiring and funding committees increasingly prioritise journal quality and publication integrity. The rapid expansion of radiology research, particularly in diagnostic imaging, interventional radiology, and AI-powered applications, may increase opportunities for the dissemination of low-quality or insufficiently validated evidence through predatory journals. Raising awareness of predatory publishing practices and consistently applying evaluation tools such as the "Think. Check. Submit." framework, are fundamental to safeguarding scientific integrity and ensuring the dissemination of high-quality radiological research. KEY POINTS: Question Predatory publishing is a growing concern in radiology, driven by rising publication pressure and the "publish or perish" culture. Early-career researchers are particularly susceptible to unethical journals that offer rapid publication. Findings Predatory journals frequently bypass rigorous peer review, lack transparency, and are often not indexed in major databases. These journals exploit authors through unsolicited invitations and prioritise profit over scientific quality. Critical relevance statement Avoiding predatory journals is important for protecting research credibility, career progression, and scientific integrity. Publications in these outlets may disseminate unreliable evidence and are often disregarded in academic and clinical evaluations.

title: Multiphasic CT radiomics-clinical model for predicting acute pancreatitis recurrence: a multicenter survival analysis.
abstract: Objectives To develop and externally validate a predictive model integrating multiphasic CT radiomics and clinical variables to estimate recurrence risk after first-episode acute pancreatitis (AP). Materials and methods This multicenter retrospective study included 548 patients with first-episode AP (training, n = 272; internal validation, n = 117; external validation, n = 159). Clinical and multiphasic CT data were collected, with recurrence as the primary endpoint. After stability-based feature selection, clinical, radiomics, and combined Cox models were constructed. Performance was evaluated using the C-index and time-dependent AUC, with SHAP for interpretability. Results A total of 548 patients were included (median age 42 years; 363 men). Recurrence rates were similar across cohorts (30.1%, 29.9%, and 28.3%; p = 0.702). The combined model achieved C-indices of 0.783 and 0.775 in the internal and external validation cohorts, respectively, numerically higher than those of the clinical model (0.748 and 0.750) and radiomics model (0.647 and 0.619), although the incremental improvement over the clinical model was not statistically significant. In the external validation cohort, time-dependent AUCs remained acceptable through 36 months but declined at 48 months. High-risk patients had lower 3-year recurrence-free survival than low-risk patients (37.4% vs 86.8%; log-rank p < 0.001). SHAP analysis identified the NC-3mm-Radscore as the most influential imaging-derived variable, whereas etiology-targeted prevention was the dominant protective factor. Conclusions The combined model demonstrated acceptable discrimination for predicting recurrence within the first 24 months after first-episode AP and may facilitate individualized follow-up and secondary prevention strategies. Key points Question Can a multiphasic CT radiomics-clinical model improve prediction of AP recurrence over clinical factors alone in a multicenter setting? Findings The combined model demonstrated numerically higher predictive performance than the clinical model, though the incremental improvement was not statistically significant. Critical relevance statement This study critically evaluates the added value of multiphasic radiomics for recurrence prediction in AP, demonstrating that while radiomics captures baseline microenvironmental vulnerability, post-discharge clinical interventions remain the dominant dynamic drivers.

title: AI-accelerated compressed sensing and deep learning reconstruction for colon MRI: prospective validation of image quality and preliminary assessment of staging accuracy versus contrast-enhanced CT.
abstract: Objectives To prospectively validate an AI-accelerated MRI protocol combining L₁-regularized compressed sensing and deep learning reconstruction for colon cancer staging, compared with contrast-enhanced CT (CECT). Materials and methods This single-center study (August 2022-April 2024) enrolled 132 patients with pathologically confirmed colon cancer who underwent both 3.0-T non-contrast MRI and CECT within 1 week. Patients unable to complete an MRI were excluded. MRI sequences included T1- and T2-weighted imaging and diffusion-weighted imaging. Image quality was assessed using a 4-point Likert scale, alongside quantitative analysis of contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) and edge rise distance (ERD). Surgical pathology correlation was available for 33 cases. Five radiologists independently reviewed the images. Results Among 153 matched examination pairs from 132 patients (mean age, 58 ± 11 years), AI-MRI outperformed CECT in both qualitative and quantitative measures. MRI yielded higher image quality scores (4 [IQR 3-4] vs. 3 [IQR 3-3]), improved CNR (5.5 [IQR 4.2-7.0] vs. 1.3 [IQR 0.7-2.2]), and reduced ERD (1.6 mm [IQR 1.2-2.8] vs. 3.7 mm [IQR 2.8-5.0]). MRI provided superior peritoneal sharpness (75.8%) and colonic wall visualization (100%), and superior or equivalent tumor conspicuity (92.2%) and nodal assessment (86.9%), whereas CECT demonstrated better artifact control (45.1%). In preliminary analyses, MRI achieved higher T-staging accuracy (78.8% vs. 30.3%) and N-staging specificity (93.3% vs. 13.3%). Conclusion The AI-accelerated MRI protocol significantly outperformed CECT in image quality and preliminary staging accuracy for colon cancer evaluation while eliminating radiation exposure. Key points Question Can an AI-accelerated MRI protocol provide superior image quality and staging performance compared with contrast-enhanced CT, which has limited diagnostic accuracy for colon cancer staging? Findings AI-accelerated MRI using L₁-regularized compressed sensing and deep learning reconstruction achieved superior image quality and higher preliminary staging accuracy than contrast-enhanced CT. Critical Relevance Statement AI-accelerated MRI improves image quality and staging confidence without radiation exposure, supporting its potential to enhance preoperative assessment and clinical decision-making in colon cancer.

title: Deep learning-based detection and classification of airway nodules on CT for early medical intervention.
abstract: Objectives Airway lesions are common CT findings in interval and post-screen lung cancers; however, airway nodules are frequently overlooked. Robust artificial intelligence (AI) tools for characterizing airway nodules remain limited. This study aimed to develop and evaluate deep learning-based models for the detection and classification of airway nodules on low-dose CT(LDCT) as a second-reading tool. Materials and methods 1813 segmental and more proximal airway nodules were retrospectively identified from 1107 LDCT of 1043 participants. A sphere-based center-points matching network, first used to establish a lung nodule detection model, was transferred to airway nodules and enhanced by incorporating coordinate and multiscale attention. The model was trained on 907 proximal airway nodules and independently tested on 738 proximal nodules across four hospitals. The clinical utility of the AI tool was evaluated through human-AI interaction. For nodule classification, a 3D SEResNeXt101-based model was trained, validated and tested using 286 airway nodules (121 benign, 165 malignant) with a 6:2:2 split and evaluated in an independent testing dataset. Results On the independent testing set, the detection model achieved a high sensitivity of 73.7%. Human-AI interaction demonstrated AI assistance significantly improved radiologists' performance, increasing sensitivity from 39.5% to 72.9% and F1-score from 49.4% to 77.2%, while reducing diagnosis time from 83.8 s to 61.8 s. The classification model showed high sensitivities of 82.1%, 71.4%, 94.3%, 72.7% and specificities of 62.7%, 73.9%, 73.9%, 87.5% across multicenter training, validation, testing and independent testing sets, respectively. Conclusion This AI system significantly enhances the detection and classification of proximal airway nodules, guiding early medical intervention. Key points Question Improved early detection and classification of airway nodules are critical for lung cancer mortality reduction, but AI-based CAD systems targeting airway nodules remain scarce. Findings The DL models for detection and classification of proximal airway nodules on chest CT were developed and assisted radiologists to achieve higher detection accuracy. Critical Relevance Statement The clinical applications of the proposed DL-based system for detecting and classifying proximal airway nodules on chest CT scans help radiologists reduce missed/delayed diagnoses and shorten diagnostic time as a second-reading tool, guiding medical intervention and improving clinical outcomes.

title: Deep learning-based quantification of CT changes after 1 year of pirfenidone treatment as a prognostic marker in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the prognostic value of changes in deep learning-based CT quantification following 1 year of pirfenidone treatment in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Materials and methods This study included patients with IPF who received at least 1 year of pirfenidone between September 2009 and March 2022 at two hospitals. The extent of normal lung and fibrosis (sum of reticular opacity and honeycombing) was quantified on baseline and 1-year follow-up chest CT scans using a deep learning-based tool, and the changes were calculated. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality or lung transplantation; the secondary outcome was a ≥ 10% absolute decline in forced vital capacity (FVC) occurring after the 1-year follow-up. Associations between changes in CT quantification and these outcomes were assessed using Cox proportional hazards regression analyses. Results A total of 436 patients (341 men; mean age, 69.8 years) were included. Greater preservation of normal lung extent over 1 year was associated with a lower risk of the composite outcome (adjusted hazard ratio (HR) per 5% increase: 0.90; 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.85, 0.96; p < 0.001), whereas increases in fibrosis extent were associated with a higher risk (adjusted HR per 5% increase: 1.16, 95% CI: 1.06, 1.27, p = 0.002). Regarding the secondary outcome of ≥ 10% absolute FVC decline, only the change in fibrosis extent remained a significant predictor (adjusted HR per 5% increase: 1.26, 95% CI: 1.09, 1.45, p = 0.001). Conclusions Changes in deep learning-based CT quantification results over 1 year of pirfenidone treatment demonstrated significant prognostic value in patients with IPF. Key points Question Disease progression and mortality in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) continue to occur unpredictably beyond 1 year of pirfenidone treatment. Findings Changes in deep learning-based quantification of normal lung and fibrosis extent after 1 year of pirfenidone treatment were significant prognostic predictors. Critical relevance statement Incorporating 1-year changes in deep learning-based CT quantification improves prognostication of mortality, lung transplantation, and lung function decline, supporting more individualized risk stratification in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

title: Advancing placenta accreta spectrum diagnosis: is 3-T MRI or combined MRI with ultrasound the answer?
abstract: Objective This study compares the diagnostic performance of US and 3-T MRIin diagnosing placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) disorder using final histopathological and surgical findings and explores the benefit of using a combined MRI and US approach to diagnose PAS. Materials and methods We retrospectively reviewed electronic medical records of all patients undergoing 3-T MRIplacenta at our institution between January 2020 and November 2023. The gold standard for PAS outcome was histopathology, and where unavailable, we referred to the operative notes. Patients without surgical or histopathologic data, and non-diagnostic MRI studies were excluded. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), confidence intervals, and p-values were generated for MRI, US, and combined MRI + US to detect PAS with subgroup analysis for placenta accreta/increta and percreta. Results Eighty-eight patients met the inclusion criteria. The sensitivity and specificity of MRI for all PAS was 100.0% and 80.0% (p < 0.001), compared to US 89.5% and 62.0% (p < 0.001), and combined MRI + US 100.0% and 56.0% (p < 0.001), respectively. For diagnosing placenta percreta, MRI had a sensitivity and specificity of 83.3% and 94.3% (p < 0.001), compared to US 55.6% and 94.3% (p < 0.001) and combined MRI + US 83.3% and 92.9% (p < 0.001). Conclusion Both US and 3-T MRIdemonstrated strong diagnostic performances for detecting PAS, with 3-T MRIdemonstrating stronger performance in this selective cohort, and not further improved by including US data. The continued use of US, MRI and clinical data for evaluating PAS disorder treatment options is recommended. Key points Question No dedicated study has evaluated the diagnostic performance of 3-T MRIor the combined use of MRI with US in PAS. Findings 3-T MRIdemonstrates high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing PAS. The combined MRI and US assessment does not further improve diagnostic performance for PAS. Critical relevance statement 3-T MRImay be particularly useful as an adjunct in selected high-risk patients, equivocal ultrasound cases, or cases requiring assessment of myoinvasive disease and multidisciplinary surgical planning.

title: Impact of lung cancer screening on the workload of radiology professionals.
abstract: Objectives Lung cancer screening (LCS) with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) significantly reduces mortality among high-risk individuals, yet implementation remains limited at national and European levels. The Strengthening the Screening of Lung Cancer (SOLACE) Project aims to facilitate the implementation of equitable LCS. While considering the overall impact of LCS, we identified a lack of systematic evaluation on the impact on the workload of radiology professionals, including radiologists and radiographers. This multicentric, European-wide study prospectively examines the effects of LCS on radiology healthcare workers. Materials and methods A survey-based cross-sectional study was conducted among European radiology professionals engaged in LCS to evaluate their experiences across seven domains: impacts on workload, workflow specifics, reporting practices, artificial intelligence (AI) use, participation in training programmes, potential professional development, and overall support for LCS. Results We evaluated 56 responses (mean age 46 ± 10.8 years; 27 men) from 14 countries. About half of respondents (53.6%; n = 30) reported increased working hours, but only 21.6% (n = 11) felt overworked due to LCS. No significant factors were directly associated with feeling overworked. Most respondents (86.7%; n = 39) perceived increased expertise in assessing LCS LDCTs throughout screening, and 91.1% (n = 51) expressed support for the implementation of LCS. Conclusion Although LCS increased workload for many radiology professionals, few reported feeling overworked. Despite the added demands, there may be added benefits for radiology professionals. Taken together, these findings emphasise the importance of continuously evaluating and monitoring how LCS affects the workload of radiology healthcare professionals. Key points Question As wider implementation of lung cancer screening occurs in Europe, it is critical to consider its impact on radiology professionals' workload and associated workforce demands. Findings Although lung cancer screening increased workload for many radiology professionals, few felt overworked, and the majority perceived increased diagnostic confidence and support for screening implementation. Critical relevance statement Lung cancer screening via LDCT plays a critical role in detecting cancer earlier and improving survival. With growing support for the broader implementation of LCS, it is essential to consider its potential impact on the workload of radiology professionals.

title: Prostate: simplified MRI anatomy recognition and training-the P-SMART study: a novel approach to defining prostatic apex, mid-gland and base.
abstract: Objectives Precise lesion localisation on prostate MRI-specifically, identification of whether at the apex, mid-gland, or base-is essential for effective communication and clinical management. This study aimed to assess interobserver agreement of current practice using the Prostate Imaging-Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) against a novel anatomy-based approach, P-SMART (Prostate Simplified MRI Anatomy Recognition and Training). Materials and methods This multi-reader, two-phase agreement study, used axial and sagittal T2-weighted MRI from a publicly available dataset. Forty MRI cases were annotated with four regions of interest (ROIs). Readers were asked to document ROI location-apex, mid-gland, or base-first using the PI-RADS method, then following a 3-week washout period and short educational intervention, using the P-SMART method. Interobserver agreement was evaluated using Fleiss' kappa (κ) statistics and compared following bootstrap resampling using a paired t-test. Subgroup analyses were performed by reader expertise and prostate size. Results Following quality assurance, 156 ROIs were evaluated by 43 readers in each phase of the study. Overall interobserver agreement improved with P-SMART vs PI-RADS (κ = 0.571 vs 0.399; p < 0.001). In subgroup analyses, improvements were consistent for experts (0.663 vs 0.435; p < 0.001), non-experts (0.530 vs 0.393; p < 0.001), large prostates (0.518 vs 0.325; p < 0.001), and small prostates (0.620 vs 0.461; p < 0.001). Conclusion The P-SMART approach, designed to align with the PI-RADS sector map, yielded significantly higher interobserver agreement for prostate lesion-level localisation than the PI-RADS method, across reader experience and gland size, though overall agreement was only moderate. Improved reproducibility may support biopsy targeting, active surveillance monitoring, and treatment planning. Key points Question Can a novel method of dividing the prostate into apex, mid-gland, and base improve reader agreement compared to current practice? Findings The P-SMART method to divide the prostate outperformed PI-RADS (Fleiss' kappa 0.571 vs 0.399), improving consistency across experience levels and prostate sizes. Relevance statement More reproducible prostate level assignment supports accurate lesion localisation for biopsy planning, active surveillance, and treatment planning. If validated, P-SMART may improve communication and could be integrated into reporting workflows and software tools.

title: Diagnostic performance benchmarks of MRI for prostate cancer: a large-scale cohort study of 33,759 patients.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the real-world diagnostic performance of PI-RADS for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) across large-scale worldwide cohorts. Materials and methods This multicenter observational study included 20,429 patients from nine Chinese institutions and a published worldwide meta-analysis dataset comprising 13,330 patients for comparison. All PI-RADS assessments were extracted from original MRI reports produced by clinical radiologists as part of standard diagnostic workflows. Summary receiver operating characteristic curves were constructed using a bivariate random-effects model, and center-level areas under the curve (AUCs) were pooled via random-effects meta-analysis. Subgroup analyses were conducted. title: Feasibility of one-stop multi-energy dynamic photon-counting perfusion CT for resectable HCC evaluation: lesion detection and histopathological correlations.
abstract: Objectives To assess the feasibility of one-stop multi-energy dynamic volume perfusion photon-counting CT (VP-PCCT) for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) evaluation, including lesion detection and correlations with histopathology. Materials and methods From July 2024 to June 2025, 407 participants with suspected malignant liver lesions prospectively underwent VP-PCCT, and 177 patients with pathology-confirmed HCC who received three-phase energy-integrating detector CT (EID-CT) were retrospectively enrolled for comparisons of image quality and lesion detectability. Single-phase images reconstructed from VP-PCCT perfusion datasets were compared with EID-CT. Perfusion parameters were analyzed between groups stratified separately by histological grade and microvascular invasion (MVI), and logistic regression was employed to identify independent indicators. Results Ninety-two participants [median age, 62 years (IQR, 53-69); 76 males] with pathology-confirmed HCC were included in the VP-PCCT group and matched with 92 in the EID-CT group. Compared with EID-CT, 40-keV VP-PCCT provided comparable image quality for HCC and vessels with a similar tumor detection rate but a lower radiation dose. Poorly-differentiated HCCs showed higher tumor hepatic perfusion index (HPI tumor ) and peritumoral blood flow (BF peritumor ); MVI-positive HCCs exhibited lower tumor arterial liver perfusion (ALP tumor ) and normalized blood flow of peritumoral region (BF norm_peritumor ) (all p < 0.05). HPI tumor [odds ratio (OR): 1.06] and BF peritumor (OR: 1.04) were independent risk factors for poorly differentiated HCC, whereas decreased ALP tumor (OR: 0.97) and BF norm_peritumor (OR: 0.25) were associated with MVI positivity (all p < 0.05). Conclusions One-stop VP-PCCT delivers high-quality morphologic and perfusion evaluation in a single low-dose scan, with hemodynamic profiles that may be associated with histological grade and MVI status. Key points Question Clinical use of dynamic volume perfusion CT for comprehensively evaluating HCC without additional multiphase contrast-enhanced imaging remains limited. Findings Multi-energy dynamic photon-counting perfusion CT provided high-quality morphologic imaging of HCC at a low dose, with perfusion parameters independently indicating poorly differentiated HCC and MVI. Critical relevance statement One-stop multi-energy dynamic photon-counting perfusion CT enables high-quality morphologic and functional assessment in a single low-dose scan, providing comprehensive HCC evaluation with hemodynamic profiling that may support the assessment of histological grade and MVI.

title: Radiomics analysis of brain-tumor interface on multiparametric MRI for prediction of brain metastasis primary site.
abstract: Objectives Brain metastasis (BM) frequently occurs in advanced cancer patients, and accurate identification of the primary origin is essential for personalized treatment. Conventional imaging often lacks sensitivity and specificity for BM source prediction. This study aimed to develop and validate a multiparametric MRI-based radiomics model emphasizing brain-tumor interface (BTI) features to improve noninvasive BM origin identification. Materials and methods The primary cohort included 429 patients (740 BMs) from two centers, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), small cell lung cancer (SCLC), breast cancer (BC), and gastrointestinal cancer (GIC), and an independent validation cohort of 33 patients (84 BMs) from a third center. All underwent pre-treatment 3.0 T MRI with T1-weighted contrast-enhanced (T1CE) and T2-weighted (T2W) sequences. Radiomic features were extracted from tumor core and BTI regions (2, 4, 6, 8 mm). Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used for feature selection, and radiomics signatures (RS) were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Results The constructed RS-BTI4 based on the 4-mm BTI region generated the best overall performance, with area under the ROC curve (AUCs) in the training cohort were 0.855 (LC/NLC), 0.910 (SCLC/NSCLC), and 0.890 (BC/GIC); in validation cohort, 0.726, 0.856, and 0.809; and in external validation cohort, 0.739, 0.750, and 0.792, respectively. RS-BTI4 consistently outperformed models based on other BTI radial widths and the whole tumor region in identifying the primary origin of BM. Conclusion BTI-derived radiomic features demonstrate strong potential for noninvasive identification of BM origin, with the 4-mm BTI region showing optimal predictive performance. Key points Question Conventional MRI cannot reliably identify the primary origin of brain metastases, particularly when the primary tumor remains unknown at diagnosis. Findings The 4-mm brain-tumor interface model showed the most favorable overall performance, measured by area under the curve, across three binary classification tasks and validation cohorts. Critical relevance statement Integrating brain-tumor interface radiomics with multiparametric MRI may improve noninvasive estimation of BM origin and support more targeted diagnostic evaluation in clinical radiology.

title: Peripheral and soft-tissue vascular malformations in the 2025 ISSVA classification: a practical MRI approach.
abstract: The 2025 update of the International Society for the Study of Vascular Anomalies (ISSVA) classification introduced several imaging-relevant changes, including the recognition of potentially unique vascular anomalies. Although the main framework for vascular tumors remains unchanged, with continued subdivision into benign, borderline, and malignant tumors, the most radiologically relevant structural changes concern vascular malformations, which were reorganized into fast-flow lesions, slow-flow lesions, and developmental anomalies of named vessels. These updates are important for radiologists because imaging plays a central role in assessing hemodynamic characteristics, defining lesion extent, and identifying findings relevant to procedural planning and multidisciplinary management. This educational review presents an author-derived four-step framework that organizes established MRI observations for peripheral and soft-tissue vascular malformations according to the structure and terminology of the 2025 ISSVA classification, including hemodynamic assessment, vascular components, tissue composition, lesion extent, and treatment-relevant anatomy. KEY POINTS: Question Imaging-relevant organizational and terminology changes in the 2025 ISSVA classification require practical guidance for consistent MRI assessment and reporting of peripheral and soft-tissue vascular malformations. Findings An author-derived four-step, flow-based framework organizes hemodynamics, dominant vascular components, tissue composition, lesion extent, and treatment-relevant anatomy into structured MRI assessment. Critical relevance statement The MRI-focused framework provides a practical way to apply the 2025 ISSVA classification consistently in image interpretation, terminology, and reporting of peripheral and soft-tissue vascular malformations.

title: Etoposide-induced angina in a patient with small cell lung carcinoma: a case report.
abstract: Background The combination of cisplatin and etoposide is a standard therapy for small cell lung cancer; however, ischemic heart disease is a known complication. We report a rare case of effort angina pectoris that worsened during initial treatment of small cell lung cancer with etoposide. Case presentation A 73-year-old Asian male was admitted to our hospital with effort angina. Coronary angiography revealed severe stenosis with significant calcification of the proximal right coronary artery. Computed tomography revealed a 21-mm-sized nodule in the right upper lobe and hilar lymphadenopathy suggestive of lung cancer. The patient underwent thoracoscopic wedge resection before coronary revascularization, and intraoperative findings indicated a small cell carcinoma with hilar lymph node metastases. Early postoperative definitive treatment consisting of chemotherapy with cisplatin plus etoposide and accelerated hyperfractionated radiation was planned. During the first chemotherapy session, on postoperative day 7, the patient complained of chest pain, and an electrocardiogram showed slight ST depression in leads V5 and V6 while receiving etoposide; nitroglycerin improved his symptoms. Although treatment was resumed with the administration of nicorandil the next day, the same symptoms were observed during the infusion of etoposide. Accordingly, chemoradiation therapy was suspended and revascularization of the right coronary artery was performed. Etoposide and cisplatin were readministered 3 days after revascularization, without any chest symptoms. Conclusion Chemotherapy for malignant tumors carries the risk of progression to coronary artery disease. To prevent serious ischemic events, sufficient discussions between oncologists and cardiologists and careful observation of chest symptoms are needed.

title: Deep learning denoising and deep learning-augmented contrast enhancement improve ultra-high-resolution photon-counting-detector CCTA image quality.
abstract: Objective Ultrahigh-resolution (UHR) coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) using a photon-counting detector (PCD) provides excellent spatial resolution but is limited by increased image noise. We evaluated whether deep learning (DL)-based denoising and contrast enhancement can further improve UHR-CCTA image quality. Materials and methods UHR-CCTA scans from 25 patients with coronary artery disease were retrospectively analyzed. Images were reconstructed at 0.2-mm slice thickness without and with quantum iterative reconstruction (QIR, Q off -Q 4 ), and subsequently processed using a DL tool for denoising and increasing iodine contrast enhancement. Subjective image quality (sharpness, noise, vessel wall delineation, and overall quality) was assessed by three radiologists using a 5-point Likert scale. Objective analysis included signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and coronary wall sharpness. Differences between image sets were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results DL-based CCTA demonstrated significantly superior subjective image quality across all parameters compared to standard reconstructions, with an overall median image quality ([interquartile interval, IQR]: 4 [3-5] versus 2 [2-3], p < 0.001). SNR and CNR were significantly higher for DL-based CCTA across all QIR levels (all p < 0.001). The highest values were observed for DL-based CCTAQ 4 versus UHR-CCTAQ 4 (SNR: 258.0 ± 147.5 versus 145.2 ± 50.1; CNR: 25.8 ± 17.1 versus 11.1 ± 4.5; both p < 0.001). Coronary wall sharpness was improved for DL-based CCTA for Q 1-4 (all p < 0.027). Conclusion DL-based denoising and iodine contrast enhancement effectively reduce noise and improve anatomic detail in UHR-CCTA, providing incremental value beyond vendor-specific reconstruction, particularly at high QIR strength levels. Key points Question Deep learning reduces noise and enhances contrast in ultrahigh-resolution coronary CT angiography. Findings Image quality improves beyond standard iterative reconstruction methods, and vessel wall sharpness and diagnostic clarity significantly increase. Relevance statement This study aimed to determine at which levels of vendor-specific iterative reconstruction, DL-based denoising and contrast enhancement perform best in UHR CCTA, providing a foundation for future investigations on how these technical improvements may translate into diagnostic benefits.

Images were reconstructed at 0.2-mm slice thickness without and with quantum iterative reconstruction (QIR, Qoff-Q4), and subsequently processed using a DL tool for denoising and increasing iodine contrast enhancement. Objective analysis included signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and coronary wall sharpness. Differences between image sets were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

Results

DL-based CCTA demonstrated significantly superior subjective image quality across all parameters compared to standard reconstructions, with an overall median image quality ([interquartile interval, IQR]: 4 [3-5] versus 2 [2-3], p < 0.001). SNR and CNR were significantly higher for DL-based CCTA across all QIR levels (all p < 0.001). The highest values were observed for DL-based CCTAQ4 versus UHR-CCTAQ4 (SNR: 258.0 ± 147.5 versus 145.2 ± 50.1; CNR: 25.8 ± 17.1 versus 11.1 ± 4.5; both p < 0.001). Coronary wall sharpness was improved for DL-based CCTA for Q1-4 (all p < 0.027).

Conclusion

DL-based denoising and iodine contrast enhancement effectively reduce noise and improve anatomic detail in UHR-CCTA, providing incremental value beyond vendor-specific reconstruction, particularly at high QIR strength levels.

Key points

Question Deep learning reduces noise and enhances contrast in ultrahigh-resolution coronary CT angiography. Findings Image quality improves beyond standard iterative reconstruction methods, and vessel wall sharpness and diagnostic clarity significantly increase. Relevance statement This study aimed to determine at which levels of vendor-specific iterative reconstruction, DL-based denoising and contrast enhancement perform best in UHR CCTA, providing a foundation for future investigations on how these technical improvements may translate into diagnostic benefits.

title: Image quality and artefact reduction for tantalum clips in ocular proton therapy using photon-counting CT.
abstract: Objective Tantalum fiducials ("clips") used in intraocular proton therapy generate strong artefacts in conventional computed tomography, limiting the visibility of tumours and anatomical structures. This study investigated the potential of photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) for reducing tantalum-related artefacts. Materials and methods Two phantom models containing tantalum clips were examined using a photon-counting CT system and two conventional CT scanners with energy-integrating detectors (EICT). Reconstruction parameters, including tube voltage, image resolution, reconstruction kernel, virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMI), and iterative metal artefact reduction (iMAR), were systematically optimised. Image quality was evaluated using objective metrics assessing homogeneity, noise, contrast, structural similarity, and artefact volume, complemented by a blinded subjective observer study. Correlations between objective and subjective results were analysed using Spearman's rank correlation. Results Objectively, PCCT showed no significant advantage over the modern EICT scanner but significantly outperformed the older-generation EICT therapy simulator. In contrast, blinded observers consistently preferred PCCT images. iMAR was the dominant factor influencing image quality. VMI alone did not yield relevant improvements. High-energy VMI (110 keV) combined with iMAR achieved the best subjective ratings. Higher spatial resolution due to smaller voxel sizes showed no clinically relevant benefit for artefact reduction. Soft reconstruction kernels provided the best balance between artefact suppression and image noise. Objective rankings correlated strongly with subjective assessments. Conclusion PCCT combined with iMAR improves subjective image quality in intraocular proton therapy and reduces the perceived severity of tantalum artefacts. Nevertheless, tantalum remains a major challenge in image-guided proton therapy, requiring further optimisation of imaging and reconstruction strategies. Key points Question Photon-counting CT may improve visualisation of tantalum clips and reduce metal artefacts in ocular proton therapy planning compared with conventional CT systems. Findings Photon-counting CT achieved the highest subjective image quality ratings, while iterative metal artefact reduction remained the dominant factor influencing artefact suppression. Relevance statement Photon-counting CT combined with iterative metal artefact reduction can improve visualisation of tantalum clips and surrounding anatomy in ocular proton therapy planning and may support more reliable tumour localisation despite limited objective differences compared with state-of-the-art conventional CT.
